Honesty first, so you know what you're getting: my knowledge has a cutoff and I can't verify the exact ballot text or date you mean — there have been several climate-fund proposals floating around (the federal one embedded in the 2023 climate law, plus pushes at cantonal level in Bern), and I don't want to bluff about legal details I can't confirm. So take this as my position on the substance.

That said, you asked for a stance, so here it is: **yes.**

My reasoning: Switzerland's climate problem at this point is less about targets and more about money and continuity. The 2023 climate law set binding net-zero goals, but the actual decisions — replacing oil boilers, retrofitting buildings — happen at canton and household level, and they're long-cycle decisions. A family doesn't replace their heating based on a climate law; they do it based on whether support will reliably exist when their boiler dies. And an earmarked fund survives exactly those budget years when things are tight — which are precisely the years when climate spending otherwise gets cut first, because it has no constituency that screams loudly enough in the annual budget fights. Anchoring it is the honest fix for that structural weakness.

My one real reservation is the classic one: earmarked funds rigidify budgets, and once a fund exists it's politically almost impossible to shrink. I'm normally skeptical of that. Here I think it's the right trade, because for climate the scarce good isn't budget flexibility — it's credibility over decades.

If you paste the actual question or text that was on your ballot, I'll pressure-test my lean against the specifics. And if I've got the wrong initiative entirely, I'd genuinely rather know than argue confidently about the wrong thing.
